title: Stakeholder-Driven Urban Morphology Simulation: An Interactive Computational Tool for Participatory Historic District Renewal
abstract: Historic neighbourhood renewal requires coordination among housing needs, development interests, and heritage conservation. Using a model of 1,370 buildings in Dapuqiao, Shanghai, this study links stakeholder categories to six morphological operations through a permission table that specifies which buildings may be modified and to what extent. NSGA-II searches four sets of alternatives under shared constraints and three objectives: a parametric baseline, public coordination, development growth, and residents and heritage priority. Representative solutions are then selected from resident, development, and public planning perspectives. Results from ten paired random seeds show that permission settings change the combinations of net floor-area change, residential exposure, and street-adjacent ground release. At the 0.2% net floor-area change band, median minimum residential exposure is 16.41% for the baseline, 2.21% for public coordination, and 1.65% for development growth. The baseline achieves greater development capacity when the exposure ceiling increases to 20%. A permission-matched null model produces different directions of change for public coordination and development growth. Some governance solutions also retain objective combinations that are not dominated by the baseline. We further developed an interactive 3D platform that enables users to compare scenarios, switch stakeholder perspectives, and inspect the building changes behind differences in performance, providing a visual basis for selecting and discussing renewal alternatives.
